extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novice to intermediate) interested in improving dialogue
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical techniques for writing varied, effective dialogue scenes in fiction, focusing on scene goals, character voice, pacing, subtext, and reader payoff. Includes exercises and examples to diagnose and fix common problems (e.g., logic-only debates, info-dump conversations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid only logic-based debate scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: If all your dialog scenes turn into logic-based debates between characters, that's a problem; one such scene is fine, but many become exhausting and boring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logic-based debates equate to conflict of ideas; variety across scenes is important. Aaron Sorkin-style rapid back-and-forth can be exciting in moderation, but not on every page. Watch for scenes that read like Socratic debates and consider replacing or varying them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give each scene two goals: physical and conversational
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure your scenes have two goals, a physical goal and a conversational (verbal/emotional) goal, so the scene has layered conflicts and movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A physical goal (e.g., wrestling match, walking somewhere) provides action and subtext while the conversational goal provides verbal tension. Having both creates imbalance and texture; when they conflict, scenes become more interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize emotional motivations over pure logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Most decisions are emotional rather than logical, so characters should often speak and decide from emotion rather than presenting cold, reasoned arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If characters only plan and debate logically, they may feel unrealistic. Use emotional stakes and connections to drive conversations; marketing/real-world decisions are cited as emotionally driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate character voices via pacing, accent, and attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulate pacing, accent, and attitude to create distinct character voices; these are the primary levers you can use on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitch and placement are mostly for audio, but pacing (sentence length, punctuation), accent (sentence structure and word choice), and attitude (emotional tone) can and should be varied. Example: 'What did you say?' can be rendered differently for a British nanny vs a drill sergeant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use punctuation and sentence structure as tools for pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation (m-dashes, colons, semicolons, commas, ellipses) and sentence length control how the reader experiences timing and rhythm in dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with these tools to create run-on speakers or clipped talkers. Many writers underuse punctuation options; using them deliberately can change how lines read and how distinct a voice feels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove every third line exercise to compress and naturalize dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: A mechanical exercise: remove every third line of dialog to force natural jumps and create a compressed, more naturalistic flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an exercise, not a universal fix. After deleting lines you must add bridging material (description, body language, internal thought) to cover missing beats. It helps create the sense of people anticipating and jumping ahead in conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary setting and surface action to enliven dialog
rubrics_metrics.description: Move the scene to an interesting setting or include a physical activity to give subtext and keep otherwise informational dialogue engaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Replace a boring info-transfer conversation with a wrestling match that reveals character subtext (Dalinar example). Changing location or adding action can turn a weak scene into a memorable one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide the reader a tangible reward in each scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about the reader’s reward for reading the scene; the scene should deliver some payoff (emotional, plot-wise, or sensory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a conversational scene only exists to transfer information, add a reward (staging, reveal, imagery) so the reader isn't left feeling bored. Even a hallway walking scene can be justified if it culminates in an interesting visual or revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish authorial intent from character intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that scenes serve both what the author needs (plot/exposition) and what the character wants; the character's intention must be present inside the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a scene only serves authorial intent (info dump), it will feel flat. Ensure characters have concrete aims—looking clever, getting information, preventing something—and let those aims drive the dialogue and choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use imbalances of goals and power to add texture
rubrics_metrics.description: Create imbalance—mismatched conversational goals or power differentials—so conversations are uneven and interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: parent vs teenager, boss vs employee, one character trying to learn a secret while the other resists. These asymmetries produce natural tension and characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lazy 'shot/reverse-shot' or corridor dialogue without justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes that are simply people walking and exchanging lines (the cinematic shot/reverse-shot repeated) are often lazy and boring unless there's a clear payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the scene merely transmits facts, consider summarizing or relocating the conversation to a setting that offers subtext, action, or sensory payoff. Use such formats sparingly and with purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey subtext through nonverbal action and scene choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Show character states and transformations via actions and setting rather than explicit statements; use nonverbal beats to communicate subtext.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a character trying to recapture youth shown losing in a wrestling match communicates theme without saying it. Use body language, physical stakes, and scene choreography to reveal internal states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuild context with body language and interiority when trimming dialog
rubrics_metrics.description: When you strip dialogue (or remove lines as an exercise), replace missing context with body language, internal thought, and description to make the scene coherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homework: remove all description, then every third line, then rebuild description using body language and thought. Bridging material is necessary to cover ellipses in the conversation and create flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulate word choice and sentence structure to reflect accent and class
rubrics_metrics.description: Accent and class distinctions should be conveyed by sentence structure and word choice rather than relying solely on phonetic spellings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: rendering foreign-language speech as slang/class-linked dialect in the narrator's head; a lower-class Victorian may be heard as Cockney in a Victorian narrator's perception. Use structure and diction to signal these differences.
